quiz.title: Chapter 1 Quiz: Foundations of Legal Authority
quiz.intro: Ten questions on where the law lives and which authority controls. Every answer is in the chapter; feedback names the section to reread.

items.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five primary sources of U.S. law the chapter names?
options: Treaties
Regulations
Treatises
Constitutions
items.why: Treatises are secondary sources: they explain the law but are not the law. The five primary sources are constitutions, statutes, regulations, case law, and treaties (Sources of U.S. Law).

items.q: A statute is first published as a standalone document, then gathered chronologically, then organized by subject. In order, those three forms are:
options: Slip law, session laws, code
Code, session laws, slip law
Session laws, slip law, code
Slip law, code, session laws
items.why: Slip law first, then session laws (chronological), then the code (by subject), like the United States Code (Sources of U.S. Law).

items.q: An Arizona trial court is deciding a question of Arizona law. Which authority is binding on it?
options: A decision of the California Supreme Court on nearly identical facts
A decision of the Arizona Supreme Court
A decision of a different Arizona trial court
A section of a well-regarded treatise
items.why: Only a higher court in the same system binds. The California decision, the sister trial court, and the treatise are all persuasive (The Hierarchy of Legal Authority).

items.q: A federal district court sitting in Arizona must decide a question of Arizona state law. Whose reading of that law does it take its cue from?
options: The Ninth Circuit, because it is the federal court above it
The Arizona Supreme Court, because Arizona's courts are the final word on Arizona law
The U.S. Supreme Court
Whichever court decided the most recent case
items.why: On questions of state law the direction of authority reverses: the federal court follows the state's own courts, especially its supreme court (The Hierarchy of Legal Authority).

items.q: In Rowan Companies v. United States, the Supreme Court struck down Treasury regulations, and Congress then amended the Internal Revenue Code to allow what the Court had rejected. Who had the last word, and why?
options: The Court, because courts always outrank legislatures
Congress, because the conflict was over a statute's meaning and the legislature can rewrite the statute
Congress, because tax law is special
The Treasury, because agencies implement statutes
items.why: When the dispute is about what a statute means, the legislature can respond with a new statute. Compare Texas v. Johnson, where the conflict was with the Constitution and the Court had the last word (The Interplay of U.S. Legal Authorities).

items.q: Which statement about secondary sources is correct?
options: They bind courts when written by recognized experts
They are usually where research ends
They are usually where research starts and primary authority is usually where it ends
Courts may not consider them at all
items.why: Secondary sources are the map, not the destination: you read the map to find the road, then travel the road (The Hierarchy of Legal Authority).

items.q: Li v. Yellow Cab Co. (Cal. 1975) illustrates which point about persuasive authority?
options: Persuasive authority can never change binding law
A court may draw on a body of non-binding authority to replace its own binding rule, at which point the new rule binds
Only the U.S. Supreme Court can adopt comparative negligence
Secondary sources become binding when courts cite them
items.why: California replaced contributory negligence with comparative fault by drawing on scholarship and other states' decisions; the moment the opinion issued, the rule was binding statewide (When Persuasive Becomes Binding).

items.q: Under the Supremacy Clause, federal preemption means:
options: State law always overrides federal law in areas of traditional state concern
Federal law overrides conflicting state law where Congress has constitutional power to act; it can be express or implied
States may never regulate anything Congress has addressed
Preemption applies only to patent law
items.why: Preemption can be express or implied, and where federal law sets only a floor, states may be stricter. Ask the preemption question whenever a state-law issue sits in a federally regulated area (Preemption).

items.q: The chapter's Common Pitfalls warns most strongly against:
options: Reading too many secondary sources
Treating the first source you find as the whole answer
Citing federal cases in state court
Using Boolean searches too early
items.why: A single statute or case rarely tells the full story when regulations and judicial interpretation are also in play; stopping too soon leaves a gap exactly where the governing rule lives (Common Pitfalls).

items.q: Why does the chapter say validating every authority is a required step rather than a courtesy?
options: Because citators are free
Because authorities act on each other constantly: a case can be superseded by statute, a statute struck down, a regulation invalidated
Because law professors expect it
Because unpublished opinions cannot be cited
items.why: The system is always moving: authority is created, interpreted, revised, and sometimes invalidated, so the authority you plan to cite may no longer be good law (The Interplay of U.S. Legal Authorities).

drills.title: Rank the Stack
drills.blurb: Six authorities for an Arizona trial court. Put them in controlling order and read why each sits where it does.

drills.title: Binding or Persuasive?
drills.blurb: Eight sources, one forum. Decide what binds an Arizona trial court on a question of Arizona law and what only persuades it.
